I am submitting a formal complaint regarding the conduct of a Boston Police Officer identified as Officer Flores, Badge #4194. ¶ Date of Incident: November 20, 2025 at approximately 6:00 PM ¶ Location: Friend St., Boston, Massachusetts ¶ Context: Delivery access for Ascend (state-licensed cannabis dispensary) ¶ I work as a state-licensed cannabis courier delivering for Ascend through a third-party company. As you may know, Ascend has communicated repeatedly with the Boston Police Department regarding the ongoing utility work on Friend St. and the legal requirement for couriers to maintain vehicle access to the building. Under CCC regulations, transporting cannabis products through public streets on foot is both unsafe and non-compliant with state security policy. ¶ Despite this, tonight I witnessed Officer Flores speaking to my coworker in an unprofessional and concerning manner. Officer Flores stated that he “ran these streets” and that he could tow his vehicle or issue a ticket if he wanted to, implying selective enforcement of the law based on personal discretion rather than policy or public safety. ¶ This is especially troubling because: ¶ Multiple non-commercial vehicles were parked in the 30-minute loading zone and no-parking area, yet were allowed to remain there. ¶ I personally received a $90 ticket last week for parking in that same no-parking zone. ¶ Enforcement appears inconsistent and based on the officer’s preference rather than clear standards.

On Friday, November 7, 2025, at approximately 5:12 PM, Officer Dugue, while assigned to the front desk of E18 (Hyde Park Police Station), took a domestic violence report involving an ¶ intimate partner at 94 Lodge Hill Road, Hyde Park. ¶ The victim, Karuen Aime, reported that he had been dating Ivana Charles, a Boston Police Officer, for about a year until they broke up. Mr. Aime stated that he crashed Ms. Charles ' car in August 2025 and offered to pay for the damages, which Charles declined. Aime noted that Charles had gifted him a camera, but after they broke up, she wanted Aime to pay for the car damage or return the camera. Aime declined to do either. ¶ After declining, Charles; demand for the camera or money for the car, she and her cousin, Menrika Bertrand began sending him threatening messages, including, "let me catch you in person. Either give me the money or the camera, or I'm taking what I need. I'm going to have my coworkers escort me. ¶ On November 6, 2025, Charles and Bertrand came to his house. Charles told Aime’s mother that she wanted either the camera or the money for the vehicle. When Amie’s mother (what is the mother’s name?) asked them to leave her home, they complied but continued sending threatening messages. The pair stated that they would return to his house and attempt to break in to retrieve the camera. Aime told Charles she was no longer welcome on his property, to which Charles responded I don't care; I'm coming back ¶ The domestic investigation was assigned to Sergeant Detective Stephine Gaines of the Boston Police Domestic Violence Unit. She stated she interviewed Aime, and he stated that Charles made no specific criminal threats. Gaines will be closing out the domestic investigation involving Charles. ¶ Officer Charles' actions, however, violated Boston Police Rules and Regulations 102 Sec. 3 Conduct: Employees shall conduct themselves at all times, both on and off duty, in such a manner as to reflect most favorably on the Department. Conduct unbecoming of an employee shall include that which tends to indicate that the employee is unable or unfit to continue as a member of the Department, or tends to impair the operation of the Department or its employees. The incident involved an off-duty officer, Ivana Charles, whose conduct is at issue in the investigation of the domestic incident involving Aime. This matter will be referred to the Boston Police Internal Affairs Unit for investigation in accordance with the above rules.

On today's date, January 27, 2026, I was assigned as the day shift Lieutenant, HA02.  At the 7:30 roll call, I observed that Officer Dale Kennedy was not wearing a uniform shirt.  He was wearing a fleece with his badge attached to it, and a turtleneck.  I told Officer Kennedy (the last time I saw him) that he needs to wear a uniform shirt.  Officer Kennedy explained prior that putting a uniform shirt on would have made him late for roll call, and he expected to change clothes after roll call.  I told him that he needs to appear at roll call in full uniform.  For that reason, on today's date, I was surprised to see Officer Kennedy without a uniform shirt on again, so I mentioned again that he needs to wear a uniform shirt.  I typically mention it at roll call or whenever I happen to notice that someone is wearing an unauthorized hat, no hat, or otherwise out of uniform. ¶ After roll call, Sgt. Matthew Walsh and I were in the Duty Supervisor's office.  Officer Dale Kennedy stepped into the D.S. office, and without asking permission to do so, closed the supervisor office door behind him.  Officer Kennedy expressed that he felt "targeted" because he has been on the day shift "for a long time," and he was not the only person he has seen out of uniform on the shift.  He inquired if I would prefer that he "have a shirt on, or be late for roll call?"  I thought it was interesting that he wanted me to choose out of the two options.  I told him that I want him to do both, to be on time for roll call and to be in proper uniform.  Officer Kennedy was standing there having the conversation with me while wearing no uniform shirt, and an unauthorized winter watch cap with unknown logo on the front. I spoke to officers at roll call after the recent clothing allowance being paid, and they were all put on notice to fix the uniform issues. ¶ Several other officers on my shift (and on other shifts) have been spoken to by me individually or at roll call about their appearance since I've been at C-11 (usually hats and shirts).  Not one of them besides Officer Kennedy has come into the D.S. office to complain about what they were told.  Further, it is none of Officer Kennedy's business what my communication with other officers might have been regarding their appearance.  I do not answer to Officer Kennedy, but he seems to think so.  Officer Kennedy was recently assigned to be an FTO training a probationary officer.  All officers at roll call were spoken to prior about being an example for the new officers who are in training. ¶ Officer Kennedy has issues with time management on a consistent basis (late for his shift).  But most surprising to me is that he refuses to follow my directives when he is told to show up to roll call in proper uniform.  And, he seems offended by being corrected regarding that.  Further, he seems entitled to dictate a meeting with me to discuss it while choosing the time and place to have that conversation. Also, Officer Kennedy seems to think it is appropriate to ask me to negotiate whether I want him to follow one rule, or the other, as if I am in a position to choose only one rule for him to follow.  I expressed to Captain Sweeney (C-11 Commander) my issues with Officer Kennedy, that he will be writing a Form 26 report regarding our conversation, and that my opinion he is definitely not suitable to train a probationary officer who just graduated from the Academy. ¶ Officer Kennedy failed to show up in proper uniform in violation of Rule 103 Section 3, he refused to follow my directive to show up to roll call in proper uniform Rule 102, Section 8, and he walked into the D.S. office to complain about the directive with a sense of entitlement to do so as though he runs my shift.  Officer Kennedy was disrespectful.  On one occasion, I was meeting with an officer and a supervisor in my office.  I hung a sign on the door, stating that I was busy, and indicated where to leave any paperwork or messages for me.  Officer Kennedy disregarded the sign, and interrupted the meeting by knocking on the door, simply to hand me a Form 25. narrative_x: I am submitting a formal complaint regarding the conduct of a Boston Police Department officer during an interaction on February 3, 2026, at approximately 10:00 PM, in front of 4 Ernest Ave, Hyde Park, MA (Hyde Park / East Dedham area). ¶ Due to winter conditions, snow removal was taking place, reducing a normally two-lane road to a single lane. I was behind multiple vehicles and could not see what was happening ahead. I waited for approximately 10 minutes without any movement or communication from the officer regarding traffic direction or the expected delay. ¶ At one point, the vehicle in front of me made a U-turn. The vehicle behind me then crossed into the opposite lane to continue and attempted to enter 4 Ernest St, which was not closed. I followed this vehicle cautiously to exit safely and avoid remaining stuck in traffic caused by snow removal. ¶ During this time, the officer stopped the vehicle in front of me and spoke with its driver longer than usual, then allowed all other vehicles in the normal traffic lane to proceed, leaving only myself and the driver in front held without explanation. Feeling stressed, frustrated, and wanting to go home, I briefly used my headlights to get the officer’s attention and calmly asked from my window, “How much longer are we going to wait?” The officer suddenly became angry and responded by yelling, “Whenever I want,” while allowing all other vehicles to pass. ¶ The officer then approached my vehicle with a hostile and accusatory attitude, demanding my driver’s license, while allowing the car in front of me—which initially drove in the opposite lane—to leave. I respectfully provided my license, which the officer took. He went to the other vehicle and took a long time before returning to me, continuing to allow other vehicles to pass while instructing me to stay parked in the opposite lane, not even allowing me to turn onto another street. ¶ After returning from checking my license, the officer also asked to verify my address and informed me that a citation would be sent to my home. When I asked for clarification, the officer stated, “You were driving the opposite way,” which is inaccurate, as I was only following the vehicle in front of me in a single-lane situation caused by snow removal. ¶ Throughout the interaction, I remained calm, respectful, and compliant. However, the officer’s behavior felt dismissive, unnecessarily authoritative, and intimidating. I felt singled out and unfairly treated without any legitimate reason. I also have a video recording and my vehicle’s license plate that verify my account. Additionally, I was not alone during this interaction. A female friend who witnessed the entire incident can corroborate my account of the events. ¶ My complaint is regarding the unprofessional, unfair, and intimidating conduct of the officer, not the potential citation itself. I respectfully request that this incident be reviewed and that measures be taken to ensure that community members are treated with professionalism and fairness.

allegation_x: Body Worn Camera Deployment - Officer Responsibility
narrative_x: On Monday, February 23, 2026, Officer Freeman, operator, and Officer Lopez, observer, assigned to the J201D unit, received a radio call regarding a domestic violence incident at 2 Brewer Street, Incident #262015582. Officers left the district’s parking lot and proceeded down Green Street toward Amory Street with the wagon’s emergency lights activated. The officers had the green light and entered the intersection of Amory and Green Street when their vehicle was struck by a white Freightliner SD, Mass Reg MB961, City of Boston plow truck, traveling outbound on Amory Street. The head of the plow struck the front end of the department wagon. Neither officer’s BWC recorded the accident. Their BWCs were only activated after the accident. ¶ Officer Freeman stated in his report that his BWC was in the process of turning on, which he cited as the reason it did not record the incident. Officer Lopez did not provide any explanation in his report. Boston Police Department Rule 405, Sec. 3.1 requires officers to turn on their BWC immediately following Roll Call and for it to remain on for the duration of their shift. The officers received the 911 call around 11:20 AM, midway through their shift. Both Officers should have had their BWCs turned on and ready for recording before receiving the call for service. Therefore, both officers violated Boston Police Department Rule 405, Sec. 3.1. ¶ On Monday, February 23, 2026, Officer Freeman, operator, and Officer Lopez, observer, assigned to the J201D unit, received a radio call regarding a domestic violence incident at 2 Brewer Street, Incident #262015582.
